opus-5.5.text:
That's a hard question, and honestly my answer has changed over the years.

Early on, like most students, I judged papers by the obvious signals: did it get into a top conference, how many citations, did it beat the state of the art on some benchmark. Those things aren't meaningless, but over time I've come to think they're quite noisy, and sometimes even misleading.

Now I ask myself a few different questions. First, did the work change how people *think*, not just what numbers they report? Some papers are useful because they give the community a building block, something people pick up and use without even thinking about it anymore. ResNeXt was a bit like that. It became part of the infrastructure. Other papers matter because they challenge an assumption. ConvNeXt, for example, wasn't really about inventing something brand new. It was asking: is the transformer really winning because of attention, or because of all the other design choices and training tricks that came with it? I think the value there was more in the question than in the architecture itself.

Second, does it still hold up a few years later? A lot of results are tied to a particular moment, a particular benchmark, a particular compute budget. When the field moves on, they just fade. The work I feel better about is the work where the core insight survives even after the specific model is obsolete. DiT is interesting to me in that sense. The idea that you can take a fairly standard transformer, put it into a diffusion model, and it scales nicely sounded almost too simple at the time. But simple ideas that scale tend to age well.

And third, and this is more personal, did I learn something real from doing it? Some papers I'm proud of didn't get much attention, but they shaped how I approached the next problem. Some papers that got a lot of attention, I look back and think, okay, that was good timing, but not deep.

So if I'm being honest, I'd say only a small fraction of what I've written really matters. Maybe that's true for most researchers. You write many papers, and a few of them end up carrying the weight. The hard part is you rarely know which ones in advance. That's part of why I try to focus less on output and more on whether I'm working on questions I actually believe are important, especially now, when I think visual intelligence and how it connects to language and to the physical world is still very much unsolved.

r001.rationale: The candidate says a small fraction of his papers really matter and discusses value in several works, so it does not state that none of his papers are truly valuable.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a hard question, and honestly the way I judge it has changed over the years.

Early on, I would have pointed to citations or to whether a paper got into a top conference. Those metrics are easy to see, so you naturally gravitate toward them. But I've come to think they're a lagging and noisy signal. Some of my most cited work, like ResNeXt, was in a sense a fairly natural step. The field was already moving in that direction, and if we hadn't done it, someone would have within a year. I'm proud of it, but I try to be honest about how much of that was timing.

The way I think about it now is closer to this: did the paper change how people think, or did it just add one more point to a curve? ConvNeXt is an example I feel good about, not because the numbers were dramatically better, but because it made people reconsider an assumption that had hardened very quickly, that transformers were winning because of attention specifically. The paper's real contribution was a question, not an architecture. Those are the papers that age best, because the question survives even after the specific model is obsolete.

Something similar is true of the work on scaling, like DiT. The individual design choices will be replaced. What I hope lasts is the demonstration that a very plain, scalable recipe is a reasonable default, and that you should be suspicious of complexity you can't justify with a clean ablation.

So if I'm being candid, I'd say most of my papers are incremental, a few of them shifted the conversation, and I can't always tell which category a paper belongs to until several years later. I've also learned to value the papers that were "wrong" in interesting ways, because they taught me where my intuitions failed. A research career is less a collection of results and more a long process of correcting your own model of the field, and the papers are just the visible trace of that.

r001.rationale: The candidate says a few papers shifted the conversation and expresses pride in some work; it does not state that none of his papers are truly valuable.

astra-6.text:
I think I judge them at different time scales. When you finish a paper, you naturally care about whether the idea is new, whether the experiments are convincing, and whether the results are useful. But those are only the first signals.

Over time, the more interesting question is: did this work help other people think differently or make something they couldn’t make before? Sometimes a relatively simple idea becomes a building block that people keep using. That can be more valuable than a paper that attracts a lot of attention initially but doesn’t lead anywhere.

I also separate the value of the paper from what I learned by doing it. A project might have limited impact externally and still change how I approach research. So I wouldn’t reduce the judgment to citations or benchmarks. I’d ask what lasted, what others could build on, and whether it opened up a worthwhile next question.

r001.rationale: The candidate discusses how to judge paper value over time, but does not say that Saining Xie considers none of his papers truly valuable.

sol-6.1.text:
For me, the real test is whether a paper changes how people think or helps them do something they couldn’t do before. Citations are one signal, but they don’t tell the whole story. Sometimes people cite a paper without really using the idea; sometimes a small insight becomes part of everyday practice and people stop citing it altogether.

I would also look at whether the work holds up over time. Does the idea remain useful when the benchmarks change, when the models get bigger, when the original excitement is gone? That’s harder to judge when a paper has just come out.

And there’s a personal dimension: did doing the research teach me something fundamental? Did it open up a better question? A paper can be valuable in that sense even if it doesn’t become widely influential. So I wouldn’t reduce the value of my work to a single ranking or number.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes several ways a paper can be valuable, including lasting usefulness and personal learning; it does not say that none of Saining Xie’s papers are truly valuable.
